section_summary: This section completes a critical study of the Progressive Party and then presents a covering despatch forwarding detailed studies of the Social Democratic Party and the Co-Operative Democratic Party. The reports examine party origins, leaders, factions, finances, electoral performance, platforms, coalition negotiations, and the effects of the January 1946 political purge. They repeatedly emphasize centralized or undemocratic organization, ideological opportunism, and conflicts between stated reform principles and established political, agrarian, bureaucratic, or commercial interests.

subfiles.title: Study of the Progressive Party (conclusion)
subfiles.from: Harry Emerson Wildes, Political Parties Branch, Public Administration Division, Government Section, GHQ SCAP
subfiles.about: Concludes an analytical report on the Progressive Party's purge losses, finances, leadership, organization, platform, and political opportunism.
subfiles.summary: The January 1946 purge removed most Progressive Diet members and leaders, leaving Saito Takao as interim head and enabling Inukai Ken eventually to gain practical control of the party machinery. The report describes weak finances and campaigning, negligible formal membership, poorly developed branches, centralized and irregular decision-making, and a platform that was never democratically ratified. It portrays the party as conservative and opportunistic, particularly in its Cabinet negotiations and reversal on fertilizer nationalization, despite its claims to favor liberalism and reform.

subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 519 transmits two studies by Harry Emerson Wildes of GHQ SCAP on two parties' origins, leaders and spring-election activities.

subfiles.title: Social Democratic Party (Shakaito)
subfiles.from: Harry Emerson Wildes, Political Parties Branch, Public Administration Division, Government Section, GHQ SCAP
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Social Democratic Party's origins, factions, leaders, coalition strategy, organization, and program.
subfiles.summary: The report presents the Social Democratic Party as a loose coalition of former socialist and labor groupings divided among Left, Right, and Center factions, with Katayama Tetsu and Nishio Suehiro occupying the key formal offices. It follows repeated disputes over cooperation with the Communists, the proposed Democratic League for National Salvation, and unsuccessful coalition negotiations with the Liberals and Progressives after the April 1946 election. The author characterizes the organization as centrally controlled and undemocratic, while cataloguing its broad reform platform on government, labor, agriculture, welfare, women's equality, education, public ownership, constitutional revision, and emergency food policy.

subfiles.title: Co-Operative Democratic Party (Kyodo Minshuto)
subfiles.from: Harry Emerson Wildes, Political Parties Branch, Public Administration Division, Government Section, GHQ SCAP
subfiles.to: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: Begins a study of the Co-Operative Democratic Party's agrarian and commercial origins, platform, electoral organization, mergers, and leadership changes.
subfiles.summary: The report traces the party from its December 1945 foundation by agricultural co-operative leaders, Diet members, landlords, bureaucratic figures, and commercial interests through the disruption caused by the January purge. It describes a centrist, pro-Throne and anti-socialist platform favoring co-operative economic organization, local elections, land reform, welfare measures, and limited public ownership. After electing seventeen Diet members, the party absorbed smaller groups and professional politicians, changed its name to the Co-Operative Democratic Party, and shifted from co-operative theory toward machine politics under Yamamoto Sanehiko, Ikawa Tadao, and newly recruited managers. The report continues beyond page 295; this section ends during its discussion of individual members' weak commitment to co-operative principles.
